section.title: The Plague of Boils
section.sectionRationale: A brief, sharply focused sixth plague, from Moses tossing soot into the air before Pharaoh to the striking detail that even Egypt's magicians, who had copied earlier signs, cannot stand before Moses because they too are afflicted.
section.thesis: The very magicians who once matched God's signs are now themselves covered in boils and unable even to appear before Moses, and here for the first time the text says plainly that the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, without any mention of Pharaoh's own hardening alongside it.
section.frameNote: One scene: soot tossed into the sky becomes festering boils on man and beast, striking down even Egypt's magicians, and the LORD hardens Pharaoh's heart.

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, “Take handfuls of soot from the furnace; in the sight of Pharaoh, Moses is to toss it into the air.
It will become fine dust over all the land of Egypt, and festering {{shechin|boils}} will break out on man and beast throughout the land.”
So they took soot from the furnace and stood before Pharaoh. Moses tossed it into the air, and festering boils broke out on man and beast.
The magicians could not stand before Moses, because the boils had broken out on them and on all the Egyptians.
But the LORD {{chazaq3|hardened}} Pharaoh's heart, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said to Moses.

shechin.gloss: Boils, an inflamed, festering skin eruption, the same word used of Job's affliction in Job 2:7 and later listed among the covenant curses in Deuteronomy 28:27. A painful, humiliating disease that strikes indiscriminately at man and beast, high and low.

chazaq3.gloss: To harden or strengthen. This is the first plague in the cycle where the text states plainly and solely that the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, with no parallel statement here of Pharaoh hardening his own heart, sharpening the mystery of divine sovereignty in his resistance.

basic.context: This is the sixth plague, and it is short but pointed. Moses throws soot into the air, and it becomes festering boils on every person and animal in Egypt, so severe that even Pharaoh's own magicians, who had matched earlier signs, cannot even stand before Moses because they too are covered in sores.
basic.hermeneutics: This is real history, and this passage contains one of the clearest single statements in the whole cycle that the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, without pairing it here with any mention of Pharaoh hardening his own heart in this same verse. The passage does not try to soften or explain away this tension; it simply states it.
basic.originalLanguages: The shechin, boils, is the same affliction that struck Job and later appears among the covenant curses in Deuteronomy 28. Here it strikes down even the magicians who had imitated earlier plagues, and the text says the LORD chazaq, hardened, Pharaoh's heart directly.
basic.typology: The magicians who once matched God's power now cannot even stand before His servant, a small picture of how every rival power, however impressive at first, eventually collapses before the greater power of God, a pattern completed when every knee bows before Christ, Philippians 2:10.
basic.christ: The boils, later listed among the curses for covenant unfaithfulness in Deuteronomy 28:27, anticipate how Christ bears the curse of the law for His people, Galatians 3:13, taking on Himself the full weight of judgment that sin deserves so that believers are spared it.
basic.god: God is sovereign even over Pharaoh's hardened will, and this passage does not shy from stating that sovereignty starkly. Yet He remains just, since Pharaoh had already, repeatedly and freely, chosen hardness in the plagues before this one; God's hardening here confirms rather than originates a direction Pharaoh had already set.
basic.crossReferences: Job 2:7 describes Job's own affliction with the same word for boils. Deuteronomy 28:27 lists boils among the curses for covenant disobedience. Romans 9:18 discusses God's freedom in showing mercy and hardening.
basic.oneStory: This is a sharp, almost humiliating strike in God's judgment on Egypt, striking down even its magicians, and stating plainly that the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart. It sharpens the mystery of divine sovereignty and human responsibility that Paul later addresses directly in Romans 9, a tension the Bible holds without resolving.

context.literary:
The boils close the second set of three plagues, and like the gnats at the end of the first set, they come without warning. There is no morning meeting at the river and no speech to Pharaoh, only a command to Moses and Aaron and an action 'in the sight of Pharaoh,' verse 8. The parallel with the gnats is close. In both, a handful of earth material is turned into an affliction on 'man and beast,' dust struck with a staff in Exodus 8:17 and soot thrown into the air in verse 10. In both, the magicians' failure follows at once, Exodus 8:18 and 9:11, and in both the section closes on the hardening formula. The narrator has built the two triads to end on matching notes.

Within the scene there is a small but telling chain of 'standing.' Moses and Aaron 'stood before Pharaoh,' verse 10. The magicians 'could not stand before Moses,' verse 11. A few verses later God tells Pharaoh, 'I have raised you up,' Exodus 9:16, a causative form of the same verb, 'I have caused you to stand,' which the BSB footnote renders 'Or have spared you.' God's servants stand, God's enemies fall, and Pharaoh stands only because God holds him up for a purpose.

The magicians leave the story here. They entered in Exodus 7:11 with confident imitation, faltered in Exodus 8:18, confessed in 8:19, and now cannot even appear. Their exit is quiet but final. From here on the contest is no longer between two kinds of power. It is between the LORD and a king who has no one left to stand beside him.

Verse 12 then reaches a turning point in the hardening theme. For the first time the narrator reports, as an event, that 'the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart.' God had predicted this in Exodus 4:21 and 7:3, and the closing words, 'just as the LORD had said to Moses,' point back to those predictions. From here the same statement recurs in Exodus 10:20, 10:27, 11:10 and 14:8.
context.historical:
The soot came 'from the furnace,' verse 8, a kiln used for firing bricks, pottery or lime, or for smelting. The word used, kivshan, describes a large furnace whose smoke rises visibly. It is used for the smoke over Sodom, 'like smoke from a furnace,' Genesis 19:28, and for Sinai when the LORD descended in fire, 'like the smoke of a furnace,' Exodus 19:18. In Egypt, a land of great building projects that relied on forced labour and brick, Exodus 1:14, the kiln was part of the machinery of Israel's oppression. It is fitting, though the text does not spell it out, that the ash of Egypt's furnaces becomes the instrument of its judgment. Deuteronomy later calls Egypt itself 'the iron furnace,' Deuteronomy 4:20, using a different word but the same picture.

Moses throws the soot 'into the air,' literally toward the heavens, the same direction in which he will stretch out his hand for the hail and the darkness, Exodus 9:22 and 10:21. The gesture was public and visible. Everyone present could see that the affliction came from the act of God's servant, not from the air of the Delta or a chance outbreak.

Skin disease was a grave concern in the ancient world, and Egypt was known for its medical learning, with physicians, priests and incantations devoted to healing. Deuteronomy's phrase 'the boils of Egypt,' Deuteronomy 28:27, suggests that the affliction became proverbially associated with Egypt in Israel's memory. For court magicians, whose standing rested on ritual power and whose role often included healing, being covered in sores was a public humiliation. They could neither prevent the plague nor cure themselves.

The magicians are silent here, and so is Pharaoh. There is no negotiation, no request for prayer and no concession. The silence of the court is part of the scene's force.
context.canonical:
The Hebrew word shechin, boil, ties this plague to a significant thread in Scripture. The law of skin disease addresses the boil that heals badly, Leviticus 13:18-20. Hezekiah's boil brings him near to death, and God heals him in answer to prayer, 2 Kings 20:7 and Isaiah 38:21. Job is struck 'with terrible boils from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head,' Job 2:7. And the covenant curses warn Israel, 'The LORD will afflict you with the boils of Egypt,' Deuteronomy 28:27, and 'with painful, incurable boils on your knees and thighs,' Deuteronomy 28:35.

These passages form a sobering pattern. The plague that marked Egypt as the enemy of God becomes the sign of what Israel will suffer if it becomes like Egypt. Conversely, obedience brings the promise, 'I will not bring on you any of the diseases I inflicted on the Egyptians. For I am the LORD who heals you,' Exodus 15:26, and 'He will not lay upon you any of the terrible diseases you knew in Egypt,' Deuteronomy 7:15.

The hardening statement of verse 12 is taken up by Paul in Romans 9. Quoting Exodus 9:16, 'I raised you up for this very purpose,' Paul concludes that God 'hardens whom He wants to harden,' Romans 9:17-18. He then answers the objection, 'Then why does God still find fault?' Romans 9:19, not by softening the statement but by appealing to God's rights as Creator and His purpose to make known 'the riches of His glory' to 'the vessels of His mercy,' Romans 9:23.

The book of Revelation reprises this plague. When the first bowl is poured out, 'loathsome, malignant sores broke out on those who had the mark of the beast,' Revelation 16:2. Later, under the fifth bowl, people 'curse the God of heaven for their pains and sores; yet they did not repent,' Revelation 16:11. The final judgment of the world is described in the colours of Egypt, and the hardness of Pharaoh reappears in the hardness of the last rebels.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wants Israel to see that the rival power which had shadowed Moses from the first audience is now finished. The magicians had been Pharaoh's answer to every sign. Now they are removed not by argument but by the plague itself, stricken with the same sores as everyone else. Israel would meet many claims to spiritual power in Canaan and beyond. This scene teaches that such power, however impressive, has no standing before the LORD.

The author also intends a theological statement about the hardening. By reporting in verse 12, for the first time, that the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and by tying it to what God had said, he shows Israel that Pharaoh's stubbornness was never outside God's control. God had announced it before Moses returned to Egypt, Exodus 4:21. The reader is meant to feel the weight of that sovereignty and also to see its purpose, which Exodus 9:16 states: so that God's power would be displayed and His name proclaimed in all the earth.

Finally, the author prepares Israel for its own covenant life. The boils of Egypt will reappear in Deuteronomy 28 as a warning to Israel. By recording this plague, Moses gives Israel a picture of what it looks like to be on the wrong side of the LORD, so that they would fear Him and walk in His ways.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes a unique judgment and a unique act of hardening in the history of redemption. It does not teach that every illness is a punishment for a particular sin. Job's boils, Job 2:7, came on a man God Himself called blameless, and Jesus rejected the assumption that suffering always reflects the sufferer's guilt, John 9:2-3. Believers should not read their own or others' sickness as a sign of God's hostility.

Nor does the passage invite anyone to judge that a particular person has been hardened by God and is beyond hope. Pharaoh's case is presented to us through divine revelation; we have no such knowledge about the people around us. What the passage prescribes is a posture: fear of the LORD, humility before His sovereignty, and an urgent response to His word. 'Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts,' Hebrews 3:7-8. The hardening of Pharaoh is recorded as a warning, and the right response to it is to seek softness of heart while God is calling.

debates.question: Does this verse, with no mention of Pharaoh's own hardening, tip the balance toward divine determinism?

views.label: Read within the whole cycle
views.case: Earlier verses record Pharaoh hardening his own heart, Exodus 8:15 and 8:32, and later he does so again, Exodus 9:34, where it is called sin. Exodus 9:12 does not cancel that pattern. The narrative describes one complex reality from two angles, and Pharaoh remains fully responsible for resistance he chose repeatedly.

views.label: A judicial hardening after repeated self hardening
views.case: Some read an escalation. After five plagues in which Pharaoh hardened himself or his heart simply 'was hardened,' God now confirms him in the path he chose. This is a judgment in which God gives a person over to his own desires, a pattern Paul describes in Romans 1:24 and 1:28.

views.label: God's sovereignty is primary from the start
views.case: Others note that God announced the hardening before any plague, Exodus 4:21 and 7:3, and that Paul draws from this narrative the conclusion that God 'hardens whom He wants to harden,' Romans 9:18. On this view God's decree underlies the whole sequence, even the moments when Pharaoh is the subject.

debates.bearing: All three views agree that Pharaoh is guilty and that God is sovereign. The text holds both without explaining how they fit, and a faithful reading will not surrender either one.

debates.question: Does Romans 9 use Pharaoh to speak of eternal destiny or of God's purpose in history?

views.label: Individual election and reprobation
views.case: Many in the Reformed tradition, following Augustine and Calvin, read Romans 9 as teaching God's free choice of individuals for salvation or judgment. Pharaoh, alongside Jacob and Esau, Romans 9:13, illustrates that God's mercy depends 'not on man's desire or effort,' Romans 9:16, and the language of vessels of wrath and mercy, Romans 9:22-23, points beyond earthly roles.

views.label: God's freedom to use nations and people in redemptive history
views.case: Other interpreters argue that Paul's concern in Romans 9 to 11 is the place of Israel and the Gentiles in God's plan. Pharaoh is cited as one whom God used in history to display His power, as Exodus 9:16 states. Paul's argument ends not in reprobation but in God's purpose 'that He may have mercy on everyone,' Romans 11:32.

debates.bearing: Both readings take God's sovereignty seriously and both stress human responsibility. Whichever is preferred, Exodus 9:12 shows that God's purposes are never thwarted by human resistance, and Romans 9 insists that the right response is not accusation of God but trust in His mercy.

study.originalLanguages:
The word for boil, shechin, is thought to come from a root meaning to be hot or inflamed, which fits the burning sores it describes. It appears in the law of skin diseases, Leviticus 13:18-20, in the illness of Hezekiah, 2 Kings 20:7, in Job 2:7, and in the curses of Deuteronomy 28:27 and 28:35. The Greek translation of Exodus rendered it with a word for an ulcer or sore, and the same Greek word appears in Revelation 16:2 for the 'loathsome, malignant sores' of the first bowl, and in Luke 16:21, where the dogs licked the sores of Lazarus. The link between Exodus and Revelation is therefore verbal as well as thematic.

The boils are described as 'festering,' verse 9, literally breaking out in blisters. The verb here, meaning to break out or sprout, is the same verb used when skin disease 'breaks out all over his skin,' Leviticus 13:12, and when an infection 'has broken out in the boil,' Leviticus 13:20. In the ordinary sense the verb is used of plants blossoming. The picture is of something bursting through the skin.

The soot of verse 8 becomes 'fine dust,' verse 9. The effect is to connect this plague with the gnats of Exodus 8:16-17, where the dust of the earth became insects. Two plagues at the end of the two triads begin from particles of earth or ash, and both land on 'man and beast.' The repetition invites the reader to see the second as a heavier version of the first.

The verb 'stand' in verse 11 is amad, used of taking one's place before a superior. The magicians 'could not stand before Moses,' where yakhol, to be able, repeats the 'could not' of Exodus 8:18. Then in Exodus 9:16 God says, 'I have raised you up,' using the causative of the same verb amad. The magicians cannot stand; Pharaoh stands only because God keeps him standing. When Paul quotes the line in Romans 9:17 he uses a Greek verb meaning 'I raised you up,' which highlights God's purpose in Pharaoh's rise.

In verse 12 'hardened' is chazaq in its intensive form, with the LORD as subject: 'the LORD strengthened' or 'made firm' Pharaoh's heart. The BSB footnote offers 'stiffened or strengthened.' The verb is the one used positively for courage elsewhere, but here it describes a heart made firm in resistance. Across Exodus three verbs describe the hardening: chazaq, to make firm; kaved, to make heavy, as in Exodus 8:15 and 9:7; and qashah, to make hard or stubborn, used in Exodus 7:3. The variety is part of the narrator's portrait of a heart that resists from every side.

typology.type: The magicians unable to stand before God's servant, Exodus 9:11
typology.fulfillment: The magicians had matched Moses step for step, but in the end they could not even stand in his presence. The Psalms ask, 'When You are angry, who can stand before You?' Psalm 76:7, and Revelation asks the same of the day of wrath, 'who is able to withstand it?' Revelation 6:17. In Christ every rival power is finally brought low, for God has given Him 'the name above all names,' so that every knee will bow, Philippians 2:9-11. The type falls short because the magicians fell before a man; all creation will bow before the Son.

typology.type: The boils of Egypt and the curse of the covenant
typology.fulfillment: The boils became the sign of what a covenant breaker would suffer, Deuteronomy 28:27. Christ entered that curse in His own body. 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13. Isaiah foresaw one who would be 'stricken by God,' and by whose stripes we are healed, Isaiah 53:4-5, and Matthew applies that prophecy to Jesus' healing ministry, Matthew 8:17. The escalation is that He not only removes sickness but bears the guilt that lies beneath it. The type falls short because Egypt's boils were judgment without remedy, while Christ's wounds bring healing.

typology.type: Pharaoh raised up to display God's power, Exodus 9:16
typology.fulfillment: God kept Pharaoh standing so that His name would be proclaimed in all the earth. In Christ the display of God's power reaches its height, not in the defeat of an enemy king but in the cross and resurrection. At the cross 'He made a public spectacle' of the powers, Colossians 2:15, and in the resurrection God declared Jesus to be the Son of God 'with power,' Romans 1:4. The escalation is that the display now brings salvation to the nations. The type falls short because Pharaoh was a reluctant instrument, while Christ offered Himself willingly.

study.christ:
The boils lead to Christ first through the theme of the curse. Deuteronomy turns the plague on Egypt into a covenant sanction on Israel: 'The LORD will afflict you with the boils of Egypt,' Deuteronomy 28:27. The sign of God's enemy becomes the sign of a covenant broken. Paul declares that 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13. The one who never deserved any of the curses of Deuteronomy took their full weight so that His people would be free.

It leads to Christ through the theme of healing. The LORD who struck Egypt with boils calls Himself at Marah 'the LORD who heals you,' Exodus 15:26. In the Gospels Jesus shows that same authority with compassion. He touches a leper, reaching out His hand, and says, 'I am willing. Be clean!' Mark 1:41. He heals the ten lepers who cry out, 'Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!' Luke 17:13. Matthew sees in these acts the fulfilment of Isaiah: 'He took on our infirmities and carried our diseases,' Matthew 8:17. Peter makes the deepest connection, 'By His stripes you are healed,' 1 Peter 2:24, placing the healing in the cross itself.

It leads to Christ by contrast in the matter of standing. The magicians could not stand before Moses. Jesus stood before a Roman governor and before the high priest, silent and unafraid. He could have called on 'more than twelve legions of angels,' Matthew 26:53, and did not. And because He stood in our place, believers who could never stand before God on their own are now able to stand in grace, Romans 5:2, and will one day be presented 'unblemished in His glorious presence,' Jude 1:24.

It also leads to Christ through the hardening. John's Gospel, reflecting on the unbelief that met Jesus' signs, quotes Isaiah: 'He has blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts,' John 12:40. The pattern of Exodus 9:12 recurs at the coming of the Son. Yet in Christ hardening is not the last word. Paul says that Israel's hardening is 'in part,' until the full number of the Gentiles comes in, Romans 11:25, and the purpose of God is 'that He may have mercy on everyone,' Romans 11:32.

The typology must stay within bounds. The boils are not a direct prophecy of Christ, and the soot of the furnace is not a coded image of His passion. The connection comes through the covenant curse, the healing power of God, and the New Testament's own reading of the hardening. In each, Christ answers the problem the plague lays bare.
study.god:
The passage shows first that God is sovereign over the human heart. Verse 12 states it plainly: 'the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart.' God had said He would, Exodus 4:21, and He did. This is not presented as God reluctantly allowing what He could not prevent. Nor is it presented as God creating evil in an innocent man. Pharaoh had hardened himself repeatedly, Exodus 8:15 and 8:32. God's act here is judicial, confirming in Pharaoh what Pharaoh had chosen. Scripture elsewhere speaks of God 'giving over' people to their desires, Romans 1:24, and that is the shape of His action here.

Second, God's sovereignty serves His glory and His mercy. Exodus 9:16 explains the purpose: 'that I might display My power to you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth.' The hardening is not an end in itself. It keeps the contest going until God's name is known among the nations, and it leads to the rescue of Israel. Paul draws the same line in Romans 9:22-23, where God's patience with the vessels of wrath serves to make known 'the riches of His glory' to the vessels of mercy.

Third, God is the Lord of health and sickness. He sends the boils and He heals. 'I am the LORD who heals you,' Exodus 15:26. He is not indifferent to human suffering, but He is not bound by it either. Disease, like every other power in creation, serves Him.

Fourth, God humbles false power. The magicians fall silent and disappear. The God of Israel does not compete with rivals on equal terms. He removes them. Daniel 4:35 captures the point in the words of a humbled king: 'There is no one who can restrain His hand or say to Him, What have You done?'

Fifth, the passage holds a real tension that Scripture refuses to dissolve. God hardens, and Pharaoh is guilty. Paul voices the objection, 'Then why does God still find fault?' Romans 9:19, and answers first with the Creator's right, 'who are you, O man, to talk back to God?' Romans 9:20. The answer is not an explanation of how the two truths fit, but an invitation to trust the character of the God who holds them both.

For worship, this passage calls believers to humility and gratitude. If God were not sovereign over hard hearts, no one would be saved, for every heart is hard by nature, Ephesians 2:1-3. The God who confirmed Pharaoh in hardness is the God who promises to 'remove your heart of stone,' Ezekiel 36:26. The same sovereignty that frightens also saves.

crossReferences.note: Before Moses returns to Egypt, God says, 'I will harden his heart so that he will not let the people go.' Exodus 9:12 is the first narrated fulfilment of that word, which is why it closes, 'just as the LORD had said to Moses.' The hardening was announced before any plague began.

God tells Pharaoh, 'I have raised you up for this very purpose.' The verb is a causative of the one used when the magicians 'could not stand' in verse 11. The magicians fall, while Pharaoh is kept standing only so that God's power and name may be displayed.

After the hail Pharaoh 'sinned again and hardened his heart.' Placed after the LORD's hardening in verse 12, this verse shows that God's act does not remove Pharaoh's guilt. The narrative calls his hardening sin even after God has begun to harden him.

At Marah God promises not to bring on Israel the diseases He inflicted on the Egyptians, 'For I am the LORD who heals you.' The God who struck Egypt with boils reveals Himself to His people as their healer, conditional on their listening to Him.

'The LORD will afflict you with the boils of Egypt.' The plague on Egypt becomes a covenant curse for a disobedient Israel. The line between God's people and God's enemies is not ethnic but covenantal; Israel can come under Egypt's judgment by walking in Egypt's ways.

Job is struck with terrible boils from head to foot. The same word as Exodus 9:9 is used, but Job's suffering is not punishment for sin. Placing the two side by side guards against assuming that every such affliction is a sign of God's judgment.

Hezekiah's boil brings him near to death, and God heals him in answer to prayer. The affliction that marked Egypt's judgment becomes, in a king who turns to God, the occasion of mercy. Isaiah 38:21 records the same healing.

Paul quotes Exodus 9:16 and concludes that God 'hardens whom He wants to harden.' He draws directly on this plague narrative to show that God's purposes in salvation rest on His free mercy, not on human desire or effort.

The first bowl brings 'loathsome, malignant sores' on those who worship the beast. The final judgment is described with Egypt's sixth plague, and the Greek word for sores matches the Greek translation of Exodus 9:9. Egypt's judgment becomes a preview of the world's.

People 'curse the God of heaven for their pains and sores; yet they did not repent.' The hardness of Pharaoh reappears at the end of history. Suffering alone does not bring repentance, then or now, which is why the gospel calls for a new heart.

Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. The boils of Egypt entered Israel's covenant curses in Deuteronomy 28, and Christ bore those curses on the cross, so that His people are freed from the judgment the plague represented.

Jesus heals all the sick, fulfilling Isaiah's word, 'He took on our infirmities and carried our diseases.' The God who struck Egypt with sores comes in Christ to heal them, and the healing points to the deeper work of bearing sin.

study.oneStory:
In the beginning God made human beings whole, body and soul, and called His work very good, Genesis 1:31. Disease was no part of that first world. After the fall, death entered and the body became subject to decay, Genesis 3:19. The boils of Egypt are one vivid instance of that fallen condition, now turned into a direct act of judgment against a king who has set himself against God.

The sixth plague also sharpens a question that runs through the whole Bible: how can God be sovereign over human hearts and still hold people responsible? Exodus does not answer it with a formula. It shows Pharaoh hardening himself, and God hardening him, and Pharaoh sinning, all in the same story. The rest of Scripture keeps that tension, from Isaiah's commission to make the hearts of the people calloused, Isaiah 6:10, to the unbelief that met Jesus' signs, John 12:40, to Paul's reflections in Romans 9 to 11.

The boils then move into Israel's covenant, Deuteronomy 28:27, becoming a warning to God's people. Israel's history bears out that warning, as the nation repeatedly took Egypt's path and met Egypt's judgments. The problem the plagues exposed was never only Pharaoh's. It is the human heart.

In Christ the story turns. He comes as the healer, touching the diseased and making them clean, Mark 1:41. He takes the covenant curse on Himself, Galatians 3:13. By His stripes His people are healed, 1 Peter 2:24. And through the Spirit He gives what Pharaoh never had, a new heart, Ezekiel 36:26.

The story does not end with judgment. Revelation shows sores poured out again at the end, Revelation 16:2, and the same hardness, Revelation 16:11. But beyond the bowls of wrath lies a city where 'there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' Revelation 21:4, and where 'the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations,' Revelation 22:2. The boils of Egypt will have no place there. The God who once struck bodies in judgment will have healed His people completely and forever.

quiz.q: How did Moses initiate this sixth plague?

options.text: He poured water from the Nile onto the ground.
options.note: That action belongs to the first plague, not this one.

options.text: He performed no action at all.
options.note: A specific action, tossing soot into the air, is explicitly described.

options.text: He struck the ground with his staff.
options.note: The staff is used in other plagues, but this specific plague begins with soot tossed into the air.

options.text: He tossed handfuls of soot from a furnace into the air before Pharaoh.
options.note: Verses 8 to 10 describe this exact action commanded by the LORD.

quiz.q: What happened to Pharaoh's magicians during this plague?

options.text: They are not mentioned in this passage.
options.note: Their affliction and inability to stand before Moses is explicitly recorded in verse 11.

options.text: They fled Egypt entirely.
options.note: The text describes them being physically unable to stand before Moses due to the boils, not fleeing the country.

options.text: They could not stand before Moses because the boils had broken out on them too.
options.note: Verse 11 records that the magicians themselves were afflicted and rendered unable to appear before Moses.

options.text: They successfully replicated the sign once again.
options.note: They are not recorded as replicating anything here; instead, they are incapacitated by the same affliction.

quiz.q: What is distinctive about the language of hardening in verse 12 compared to some earlier plagues?

options.text: It says the heart of the magicians was hardened, not Pharaoh's.
options.note: The hardening is specifically attributed to Pharaoh's heart, not the magicians'.

options.text: It says only that Pharaoh hardened his own heart, with no mention of the LORD.
options.note: The text explicitly attributes the hardening to the LORD in this verse, not solely to Pharaoh.

options.text: It states directly that the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, without a parallel mention of Pharaoh hardening his own heart in this verse.
options.note: This directness is notable compared to earlier verses like 8:15 and 8:32, which explicitly describe Pharaoh hardening his own heart.

options.text: No hardening language appears in this passage.
options.note: Hardening language is explicit and central to verse 12.

quiz.q: What other biblical passages use the same Hebrew word for boils found in this plague?

options.text: No other passage uses this same word.
options.note: The word shechin appears meaningfully in both Job 2:7 and Deuteronomy 28:27.

options.text: This word appears only once in the entire Bible.
options.note: The same word appears in at least Job 2:7 and Deuteronomy 28:27, among other places.

options.text: Job's own affliction in Job 2:7 and the list of covenant curses in Deuteronomy 28:27.
options.note: Both passages use the same Hebrew word, shechin, tying this plague to broader biblical themes of suffering and covenant curse.

options.text: Only the plagues of Revelation use this word.
options.note: While Revelation describes similar afflictions, the specific Hebrew word shechin connects most directly to Job and Deuteronomy.

quiz.q: What broader theological tension does this brief plague narrative sharpen?

options.text: This passage raises no significant theological tension.
options.note: This is widely recognized as one of the sharper statements of divine sovereignty in the entire hardening theme.

options.text: Whether Egypt actually worshiped multiple gods.
options.note: While Egyptian polytheism is relevant background to the plagues generally, this specific passage centers on the hardening language, not a survey of Egyptian religion.

options.text: The exact chemical composition of the boils.
options.note: The text is not concerned with a scientific or medical explanation of the affliction.

options.text: The mystery of God's sovereignty in hardening a heart alongside genuine human responsibility for sin.
options.note: The stark statement that the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, without qualification here, intensifies this tension that Paul later addresses in Romans 9.

questions: The magicians who once matched God's power were now unable even to stand before Moses. What rival sources of confidence in your own life eventually prove powerless before God?

This passage states plainly that the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, a hard truth Scripture does not soften. How do you hold together trust in God's sovereignty with the real responsibility you carry for your own choices?

Boils later appear among the curses for covenant unfaithfulness in Deuteronomy 28. How does knowing Christ bore the curse of the law for you change how you view painful seasons of discipline or consequence?

Even Egypt's most skilled and resistant advisers were finally silenced by this plague. Where do you need to trust that every opposing voice or power in your life will ultimately be silenced before God?

This is one of the plainer statements of divine hardening in all of Scripture, and it is not explained away. What hard truth about God have you been avoiding wrestling with honestly in your own faith?

translationNotes.note: The Hebrew shechin, boils, describes an inflamed, festering skin eruption, the same term used of Job's suffering in Job 2:7 and later listed among the curses for covenant unfaithfulness in Deuteronomy 28:27.

This is the first plague where the text states the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart without a parallel clause describing Pharaoh hardening his own heart in the same verse, a detail much discussed in the theological debate over divine sovereignty and human responsibility.
